To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
water in PEG-, PVP-, and gelatin-water system is heterogeneous in mobility.

the mobility of water in PEG-, PVP-, and gelatin-water solutions is affected by the concentration of these polymers, and that the dielectric relaxation time and spin-lattice relaxation times are useful tools for determining the mobility of water molecules in these systems.

the dielectric relaxation and NMR spectroscopy results are in agreement and show the presence of highly mobile water with mobility close to that in bulk water and of bound water with a restricted mobility in polymer-water systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of polymer on the mobility of water molecules in poly(ethylene) (PEG)-poly(vinyl) (PVP) and gelatin-water system.
the study of water molecules in poly(ethylene) (PEG), poly(vinyl-pyrrolidone) and gelatin-water solutions by dielectric relaxation spectroscopy, 17O-NMR spectroscopy and water activity measurement.
the mobility of water molecules in poly(ethylene) glycol (PEG), poly(vinyl pyrrolidone), and gelatin-water mixtures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the water mobility in the polymer-water system is dependent on the type of polymer, polymer concentration, and temperature.

the water mobility in the polymer systems studied is dependent on both polymer concentration and water activity, and that the water mobility can be described in terms of two populations: highly mobile water and restricted or bound water.
the mobility of water in PVP- and PEG-water systems is affected by a polymer concentration-dependent change in the dielectric relaxation time (and thus the mobility) of the highly mobile population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
water in PEG-, PVP-, and gelatin-water solutions exists as two populations of water molecules, one with a high mobility and one with a low mobility, which are associated with the polymer molecules.
the mobility of water in the gel system is less affected by the presence of the polymer than the mobility in the PEG or PVP systems.
we have shown that the dielectric relaxation spectroscopy and 17O-NMR spectroscopy can be used to study the water mobility in polymer-water systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the dielectric relaxation time and the spin-lattice relaxation times of water in polymer systems are sensitive to the presence of different populations of water, which have different mobilities and different degrees of association with polymer molecules.
dielectric relaxation spectroscopy is a very powerful tool for determining the mobility of highly mobile water.
dielectric spectroscopy can provide information on the mobility of water molecules that cannot be obtained by any other spectroscopic technique.
